title: Linear Inequalities, Absolute Value, and Desmos Shading
lead: This class covers linear inequalities: solving them, systems of them, and graphing them with shading. On the Digital SAT they appear in two shapes: solving an inequality (which value satisfies it?) and “which graph or point fits this system of inequalities?”, where Desmos saves serious time.

parts.title: Part 1 · The core idea
parts.html:
A linear equation uses an equals sign and has one answer: 3x + 5 = 20 gives x = 5. A linear inequality uses an inequality sign and its answer is a range of values: 3x + 5 < 20 gives x < 5, so every number below 5 works.

You solve it almost like a linear equation from Class 3: do the same thing to both sides to isolate x. There is one key difference: when you multiply or divide both sides by a negative number, the sign flips.

−2x>10 → divide by −2 → x<−5

Forgetting the flip is the most common error in this topic. The reason: multiplying by a negative reverses the number line, so what was larger becomes smaller. Positive multipliers keep the order; negative ones reverse it.

WordsSymbol
no more than, at most≤
at least, no fewer than≥
more than> (strict)
less than, fewer than< (strict)

Plugging in numbers. If a question asks “which value satisfies the inequality?”, substitute each choice and check. It is often faster than solving, and it is the best way to confirm algebra you are unsure about.

Zero is the best test value. It wipes out every term that contains the variable and leaves plain numbers on both sides. If the result is true, cross out every choice whose range does not include 0. If it is false, cross out every choice whose range does include 0.

Example. Which of the following describes all solutions to 5−3x≥2x−10? A) x≤3
B) x≥3
C) x≤−3
D) x≥15 Test x=0: 5≥−10 is true, so 0 must be in the answer. Only choice A includes 0. Check by solving: 5+10≥2x+3x → 15≥5x → x≤3 → choice A

parts.title: Part 2 · Systems of inequalities
parts.html:
A system like y > 2x − 1 and y ≤ −x + 4 describes a region of the plane: the points that satisfy both conditions at once. Each inequality is a half-plane, one side of a line, and the solution is where the two overlap.

Three drawing rules:

  • Strict signs (>, <) get a dashed boundary line. The boundary is excluded.
  • Non-strict signs (≥, ≤) get a solid line. The boundary is included.
  • To choose the side to shade, plug in a test point, usually (0, 0). If it satisfies the inequality, shade its side. If the line passes through (0, 0), use another point such as (1, 0).

The most common question is “which point (x, y) is a solution to the system?” Substitute each pair into both inequalities. The pair that satisfies both is the answer. With small numbers this is faster than graphing.

When one coordinate is given. Some questions give the point as (3, y) and ask what y could be. Elimination and substitution between the two inequalities do not help here. Put the known coordinate into each inequality, and each one becomes a simple limit on the other coordinate.

Example. The point (3,y) is a solution to the system y>2x−1 and y≤−x+12. Which of the following could be the value of y? A) 2
B) 5
C) 8
D) 11 First inequality with x=3: y>5
Second inequality with x=3: y≤9
So 5<y≤9 → choice C

Choice B is the trap: 5 is on the boundary of a strict inequality, so it is not included. The same method works when one of the inequalities is not linear, for example when it contains x².

Common mistake. Checking a point against only one inequality. It must satisfy both. The “half-solution” is exactly the trap answer the test builds.

parts.title: Part 3 · The Desmos method
parts.html:
Desmos accepts inequalities exactly as written.

  • Type y>2x-1 and Desmos shades the correct half-plane with a dashed boundary.
  • Type the second inequality. The doubly shaded region is the solution set.
  • For “which point is a solution?”, plot the candidate points. The one inside the doubly shaded region is the answer.

This is much faster than graphing by hand, especially with general form like Ax + By ≤ C. Desmos takes it as written, while solving for y by hand means dividing by B and risking a missed sign flip when B is negative.

parts.title: Part 4 · Inequalities in context
parts.html:
Word problems translate with the Class 3 vocabulary, plus a common-sense rule: numbers of items cannot be negative, and usually must be whole.

Translating step by step

  1. Name each variable and its unit: a = number of adult tickets, not “adults” or “cost”.
  2. Write each quantity as a term: price × number.
  3. Replace the limit phrase with its symbol from the table in Part 1.
  4. Put the limit on the correct side, then test one case you know is allowed.
Adult tickets cost $12 and child tickets cost $7, and at most $100 was spent. 12a+7c≤100, with a≥0 and c≥0
Maximum number of adult tickets: 12a≤100 → a≤8.33… → a=8

A minimum left over. When some amount must remain, subtract it from the budget before dividing.

Sana has $150. Notebooks cost $35 each, and she wants at least $20 left. What is the greatest number of notebooks she can buy? 150−35n≥20
−35n≥−130 → divide by −35 and flip → n≤3.71…
n must be whole → 3 notebooks

Round toward the side that keeps the inequality true. Here 4 notebooks would cost $140 and leave only $10, so the answer rounds down even though 3.71 is closer to 4.

Another pattern: “which system of inequalities represents the situation?” Choose the right signs (“no more than” versus “less than”) and match each number to the right variable. Testing a scenario you know is allowed, such as a = 0 and c = 0, quickly eliminates choices with the wrong signs.

parts.title: Part 5 · Absolute value: inequalities and equations
parts.html:
The bars in |x| mean “take the absolute value of whatever is inside”. The absolute value of a number is its distance from zero on the number line, and a distance is never negative.

Both −4 and 4 are 4 units from zero, so |−4| = |4| = 4. This is why an absolute value equation usually has two solutions: there are two starting points that give the same distance.

The process for every absolute value question

  1. Get the absolute value alone on one side.
  2. Remove the bars and write two statements: one with the right side as it is, one with the right side made negative. For an inequality, the second statement also reverses the sign.
  3. Solve both, then use both results to choose the answer.

Absolute value inequalities are range constraints.

InequalityMeansPicture
|x| < a−a < x < ax is trapped between −a and a
|x| > ax > a or x < −ax is pushed out beyond a or −a

The compound form below is step 2 of the process written on one line: |2x − 3| < 5 splits into 2x − 3 < 5 and 2x − 3 > −5, which together read −5 < 2x − 3 < 5.

How to solve

  1. For |Ax + B| < C: solve the compound inequality −C < Ax + B < C by isolating x in the middle.
  2. For |Ax + B| > C: solve two separate inequalities, Ax + B > C or Ax + B < −C.
|2x−3|<5 −5<2x−3<5 → add 3 → −2<2x<8 → divide by 2 → −1<x<4
|2x−3|>5 2x−3>5 → x>4
or 2x−3<−5 → x<−1

Absolute value equations. To solve |Ax + B| = C you must consider two cases, because the inside can be positive or negative.

  1. Case 1: Ax + B = C
  2. Case 2: Ax + B = −C
|2x−3|=5 Case 1: 2x−3=5 → 2x=8 → x=4
Case 2: 2x−3=−5 → 2x=−2 → x=−1
One value for two equations. What value of x satisfies both |x−3|=5 and |x+1|=9? |x−3|=5 → x−3=5 or x−3=−5 → x=8 or x=−2
|x+1|=9 → x+1=9 or x+1=−9 → x=8 or x=−10
The value in both lists is 8

Stopping after one case of each equation can miss the shared value, which is why step 3 says to use both results.

An absolute value is never negative, so |Ax + B| = −2 has no solution. If the question asks for the sum or product of the solutions, find both first: here the sum is 4 + (−1) = 3.

Desmos shortcut. Type the inequality or equation as it appears, for example abs(2x-3)<5 or abs(2x-3)=5. Desmos shades the solution of an inequality, and for an equation it draws a vertical line at each solution.
